newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Chirac seeks to boost election campaign.
newsitem.headline: France's Chirac seeks to boost election campaign.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac was poised on Tuesday to try to kick-start his centre-right government's lacklustre election campaign, with opinion polls showing the leftist opposition within striking distance of an upset win.

Chirac was expected to publish an article in 12 regional dailies on Wednesday in a risky effort to nudge bored voters into backing Prime Minister Alain Juppe's coalition for the May 25-June 1 National Assembly poll.

The opposition Socialists ridiculed the intervention, on the second anniversary of Chirac's election as president, which put the campaign on hold as debate again veered towards personalities and away from issues such as record unemployment.
"Nobody doubts Chirac will vote RPR," said Daniel Vaillant, the Socialists' number two, referring to the Gaullist Rally for the Republic party Chirac founded and which is now led by Juppe.

"If Mr Juppe is calling for help from Mr Chirac, it means that his campaign isn't going very well. So Mr Juppe's campaign is slipping, we can't see the broad outlines, we can't see any strong proposals," he told Europe 1 radio.

Many politicians said Chirac needed to explain more clearly his decision to call the election almost 10 months early -- he has said that France needs a new impulse partly to help it join a single currency from a position of strength.

But the election has allowed the left and far right to accuse Chirac of having a secret agenda of unpopular austerity measures to help qualify for the currency from 1999, or of wanting to pre-empt emerging sleaze scandals.
"The problem today is that France needs time to reform," Defence Minister Charles Millon said, explaining Chirac's April 21 dissolution. "There's no question of changing course.
"It's normal that the president should give the guidelines at parliamentary elections or draw the French people's attention towards the risks," he told Radio Monte Carlo.
Chirac, elected to a seven-year term in 1995, is meant to be above day-to-day politics, but presidents often seek to use the prestige of their office to sway voters behind their allies.
However he could end up as a virtual lame duck for five years if voters ignore his advice and elect the opposition.

The franc, the Paris stock market and bonds dipped on Tuesday, unsettled by polls showing the race tightening for the centre-right, which previously had a more comfortable lead. The CAC French share index was 0.5 percent lower at mid-morning.

The latest opinion polls on Monday showed the two sides almost level. A BVA survey gave the conservatives 40 percent of voting intentions, half a point ahead of the combined left, while a Louis Harris poll saw them level on 38 percent.
Both polls predicted the centre-right would retain a sharply reduced majority in parliament.
Two opinion polls for Paris on Tuesday showed that two of Chirac's close conservative allies would face problems winning re-election in Paris.
One survey showed Justice Minister Jacques Toubon, sometimes tipped as a possible prime minister, would be exactly level with a little-known Socialist challenger on a run-off vote.

And another poll indicated that Jean Tiberi, Chirac's successor as mayor of Paris and trying to fend off political sleaze scandals, would need a second-round run-off to retain his seat by a slim margin.
"Normally, interest increases as the vote approaches," Roland Cayrol of the CSA institute told the financial daily Les Echos, reflecting on widespread voter indifference.

"Here for the first time as a pollster, I'm finding the opposite phenomenon -- a certain interest at the start...then disappointment over a campaign judged repetitive and based on caricatures," he said.
